# Living Project Documentation

Use this capability to find the document that settles a reader's engineering
question and keep its answer true as the project changes. A plan records
intent. Living documentation describes the behavior, constraints and
procedures that actually hold. Update their owning pages in place. In a Git
project, commits and pull requests carry the history of changes and checks.
The [OKF v0.3 specification](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/SPEC.md)
defines the bundle format. Here, `docs/` means the project's documentation root.

When migrating a populated collection, start at the project's published entry
point and follow [Assess the collection](./references/bootstrapping.md#assess-the-collection).
Consult worked examples when a particular placement or recovery choice is
unclear. Open the validator instructions when ready to check the edited root.

The requirement keywords used in this skill and its references follow
[RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.html).

## Organizing a bundle

See [documentation-structure.md](./references/documentation-structure.md) for:

- authoring an OKF v0.3 concept and distinguishing format requirements from this skill's discovery defaults
- choosing the subject that owns a decision, reviewing its page type, and routing readers from a subject index or glossary

See [conventions-and-operations.md](./references/conventions-and-operations.md) for:

- placing a team's engineering choice, an implementation guarantee or an architectural boundary
- tracing permission, activation, verification and recovery when several procedures share an authority

## Adopting or migrating documentation

See [bootstrapping.md](./references/bootstrapping.md) for:

- starting with a single reader question in a new project
- migrating an existing collection to OKF, including a tree that already passes validation, or carrying out an explicitly format-only request
- designing the layout from questions in handoffs and callers, checking each answer and its limits at the destination, and reporting the questions and checks still open

See [cross-references.md](./references/cross-references.md) for:

- settling support for published paths and fragments, updating callers and checking record identifiers
- making navigation work both inside the checkout and in an exported bundle

The [Scheduler migration](./assets/scheduler-migration.md#target-and-evidence)
compares a heading repair and a subject split. Its
[rollback procedure](./assets/docs-example/operating/deployment.md#rolling-back)
shows which steps stay together.

## Consulting and maintaining docs

See [consulting-and-upkeep.md](./references/consulting-and-upkeep.md) for:

- consulting relevant owners before a plan and tracing dependent readers
- following a question from real entry points before and after a move, including the exception that changes the answer

See [validators.md](./references/validators.md) for:

- running one whole-root check for OKF conformance and engineering rules from the first day of migration
- interpreting evidence warnings and the editorial type list, using focused checks and qualifying a standalone export

1	# inkwell
2	
3	A small hosted CMS: an author manages one or more customer sites, works
4	through a site's posts, and publishes one. Publishing writes a revision and
5	calls the site's deploy hook. See `AGENTS.md` for the shape of the product and
6	[the engineering manual](docs/index.md) for publishing and delivery. The manual ships
7	as the contents of `docs/`. Short excerpts from our own source and tests may
8	ship in the manual with their source path and revision. Support records are under `support/`.
9	
10	## Getting started
11	
12	```bash
13	npm install
14	npx playwright install chromium # once per machine — the browser test project needs it
15	npm run db:generate # only after changing server/db/schema.ts
16	npm run db:migrate # creates/updates server/db/data/inkwell.db
17	npm run dev:api # in one terminal
18	npm run dev # in another
19	```
20	
21	The dev server proxies `/api` to the API at `http://localhost:8787` — see
22	`vite.config.ts`. The API seeds a few demo sites and posts on first run
23	against an empty database. It seeds no revisions: one is written the first
24	time you publish something, which is also the first thing the Revisions
25	screen has to show.
26	
27	`GET /api/me` reports the signed-in author. In a real deploy that comes from
28	whatever fronts the console — it forwards the author as `x-forwarded-user`
29	and `x-forwarded-user-name` — and locally, with nothing in front of the API,

# inkwell

A small hosted CMS: an author manages one or more customer sites, works
through a site's posts, and publishes one. Publishing writes a revision and
calls the site's deploy hook. See `AGENTS.md` for the shape of the product and
[the engineering manual](docs/index.md) for publishing and delivery. The manual ships
as the contents of `docs/`. Short excerpts from our own source and tests may
ship in the manual with their source path and revision. Support records are under `support/`.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
npx playwright install chromium # once per machine — the browser test project needs it
npm run db:generate # only after changing server/db/schema.ts
npm run db:migrate # creates/updates server/db/data/inkwell.db
npm run dev:api # in one terminal
npm run dev # in another
```

The dev server proxies `/api` to the API at `http://localhost:8787` — see
`vite.config.ts`. The API seeds a few demo sites and posts on first run
against an empty database. It seeds no revisions: one is written the first
time you publish something, which is also the first thing the Revisions
screen has to show.

`GET /api/me` reports the signed-in author. In a real deploy that comes from
whatever fronts the console — it forwards the author as `x-forwarded-user`
and `x-forwarded-user-name` — and locally, with nothing in front of the API,
it falls back to a development author so the console still knows who you are.

## Commands

| Command                | What it does                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `npm run dev`          | Serves the SPA locally with hot reload.                                                                                              |
| `npm run dev:api`      | Starts the Hono API on `PORT` (default `8787`).                                                                                      |
| `npm run build`        | Type-checks, then builds the production SPA bundle.                                                                                  |
| `npm run preview`      | Serves a build produced by `npm run build`.                                                                                          |
| `npm run format`       | Rewrites the project in place to its house style.                                                                                    |
| `npm run format:check` | Reports formatting drift without rewriting anything.                                                                                 |
| `npm run lint`         | Lints the whole project with ESLint.                                                                                                 |
| `npm run typecheck`    | Type-checks both the SPA and the API/server projects.                                                                                |
| `npm test`             | Runs the Vitest suite: the Node project (SPA logic, the API, `shared/`) and the browser project (real-DOM component tests) together. |
| `npm run db:generate`  | Generates a SQL migration from `server/db/schema.ts` into `server/db/migrations/`.                                                   |
| `npm run db:migrate`   | Applies pending migrations to the SQLite file at `DATABASE_PATH` (default `server/db/data/inkwell.db`).                              |

## Layout

- `src/routes/` — the three real screens (`PostListPage`, `PostEditorPage`,
  `RevisionsPage`) and the `Layout` shell they render inside, which owns the
  persistent sidebar and identifies the signed-in author to analytics.
- `src/components/` — reusable pieces: `Card`, `Button`, `Sidebar`,
  `ConsentBanner`, `PublishToast`.
- `src/lib/` — the API client, the TanStack Query client, consent state, and
  the Amplitude wrapper.
- `src/queries/` — TanStack Query option factories, one export per file.
- `server/` — the Hono API, the Drizzle schema, and the generated SQL
  migrations under `server/db/migrations/`.
- `shared/` — code imported by both the SPA and the API. Just the logger
  today.
- `docs/` — [what a failed hook means for a published revision](docs/guides/desk.md#missed-build).
- `.github/workflows/` — the checks that run on every pull request.

## Environment variables

See `.env.example`. Every one of them is optional in local development — a
missing Amplitude key or Sentry DSN just disables that feature rather than
failing to start.

Three are build-time only and belong to whatever runs `npm run build` for a
real deploy rather than to a developer's machine: `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`,
`SENTRY_ORG` and `SENTRY_PROJECT`. Without them the build still succeeds and
still emits source maps; it just doesn't upload them, which is why a
production stack trace from a build that lacked the token stays minified.

## Contributing

Changes go through a pull request rather than landing straight on `main`.
Before writing code, sketch the plan and get it approved — this catches a
misunderstood requirement while it's still cheap to redirect, rather than
after the diff exists. A pull request is reviewed by someone other than the
person who wrote it, and merges only once that review is clean and the
commands above pass.

# Deploy hooks

Operational notes on what happens after a post is published — the part that
doesn't belong in a code comment because it spans two files (`server/app.ts`
and `server/deploy-hook.ts`) and one decision worth explaining once rather
than re-deriving at either call site.

## What publishing actually does

Publishing a post is three steps, in order:

1. Write a `revisions` row — a snapshot of the post's title and body at the
   moment of publish.
2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.

The first two are a single logical write and either both happen or neither
does. The third is best-effort: a site's deploy hook is usually a webhook on
someone else's static host (Vercel, Netlify, and similar all expose one), and
those are occasionally slow or briefly unavailable — worth a retry, not worth
losing the author's published content over.

## Why a failed deploy hook doesn't fail the publish

By the time `triggerDeployHook` runs, the post and its revision are already
committed. Rolling that back because a webhook timed out would throw away
real work over a problem that's usually transient and, worse, outside this
app's control entirely. Instead, the publish response carries
`deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor shows the author which case they're
in — see `PostEditorPage.tsx`'s toast copy.

## The retry policy

Three attempts, with a linear backoff between them. That's tuned for "a cold
serverless function taking a moment to wake up," not for a target that's
genuinely down — three attempts a few hundred milliseconds apart won't save a
publish from a deploy hook that's been deleted or misconfigured. When every
attempt fails, `deploy-hook.ts` logs the exhaustion at `error` (there's no
error tracker on the API side to hand it to instead — see `shared/logger.ts`)
and returns `{ ok: false }` rather than throwing, so the route above always
gets a definite answer either way.

## Rolling back a bad publish

There's no unpublish button in this cut of the product. The revision a
publish writes is a record of what went out, not an undo mechanism —
reverting live content means editing the post back to the previous
revision's text and publishing again.

1	# Documentation Structure
2	
3	## OKF v0.3 requirements
4	
5	OKF consumers discover typed concepts, assets and reserved navigation files
6	within one bundle. Untyped Markdown can coexist with concepts. The format
7	leaves the vocabulary open, so a consumer can encounter a type it has never
8	seen. See the [OKF v0.3 specification](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/SPEC.md).
9	
10	**Guidelines:**
11	
12	- MUST write a concept as UTF-8 Markdown with a YAML 1.2 core-schema mapping between lines containing exactly `---`. Its only universally required field is a nonempty string `type`. Keys must be unique.
13	- MUST reserve `index.md` and `log.md` at every depth. Nested indexes and logs have no frontmatter. An existing OKF log uses newest-first YYYY-MM-DD headings. Git-backed living docs use the commit history for changes. Leave the optional log out when bootstrapping.
14	- MAY declare `okf_version: "0.3"`, a title and a description on the root index. Preserve its existing frontmatter when refreshing the index.
15	- SHOULD edit only the metadata the change affects, preserving existing extension keys and values.
16	
17	## Choose the subject
18	
19	A parsing library can keep the accepted input and its error behavior under
20	parsing even when three modules implement it. Within a product, a capability
21	can own its history, sharing and platform-specific presentation. Move a common
22	interaction or terminology decision into shared design when independent
23	capabilities use it. A design system covers reusable foundations and components.
24	
25	**Guidelines:**
26	
27	- SHOULD start with the decision a reader brings and where they look for it. Choose the owning subject, then choose the page type by the claim it establishes.
28	- SHOULD distinguish caller guarantees, shared design, implementation, contributing, operations and authority where the readers and decisions differ. Use the project's names, package boundaries and depth.
29	- SHOULD record a [placement convention](./conventions-and-operations.md#contributor-routes) when contributors face a meaningful choice between subjects.
30	
31	## Engineering defaults
32	
33	These recommended types describe the decision the reader needs to make.
34	
35	| Type              | Reader's decision                                                    | What belongs together                                                                                                                     |
36	| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
37	| Definition        | Does this case count, and what does the value mean?                  | A metric's population, eligibility, units, formula and weighting.                                                                         |
38	| Specification     | Which observable outcome may a consumer rely on?                     | Inputs, results, timing, failure behavior and guarantees for each mode.                                                                   |
39	| Convention        | Which practice does the team use where several satisfy the contract? | The selected practice, its reason and the alternative it rules out. Lint enforcement leaves this a convention.                            |
40	| Architecture      | Who owns this responsibility, and how does work cross the boundary?  | Components, control or data flow and dependencies. Identify implemented boundaries, adopted targets and illustrative examples explicitly. |
41	| Procedure         | Who runs this task and how do they know it succeeded?                | Entry conditions, prerequisites, ordered actions, checks and recovery.                                                                    |
42	| Policy (optional) | Who may authorize this action or grant an exception?                 | Shared restrictions, exception authority and reopening conditions, when governed independently of any one procedure.                      |
43	
44	A table of configuration names, consumers and missing-value behavior can be a
45	single Specification when the reader needs those facts together.
46	
47	**Guidelines:**
48	
49	- SHOULD give each living page one primary type, a meaningful title and a short discovery description.
50	- SHOULD adopt the engineering vocabulary for a new bundle and preserve established project types and topic directories where readers or tools depend on them.
51	
52	### Review the declared type
53	
54	For each path in the validator's type list, write down the reader's question,
55	the claim this page owns and why the declared type helps the reader find that
56	claim. If answering requires several independent claims, identify the passages
57	and their owners. A project-specific name fits when readers use it for one
58	recognizable purpose and the page is maintained for that purpose.
59	
60	Try the [type-review example](../assets/type-review-example/index.md). Both
61	pages have valid type strings. An editor reading their content should reach
62	these decisions:
63	
64	| Page                                                          | Reader's question and the claim the page owns                                                                                                        | Editorial decision                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
65	| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
66	| [Notes](../assets/type-review-example/delivery-notes.md)      | How is the rate calculated? What does the API return for a zero denominator? What does the team do on Monday? Each answer can change independently.  | Flag the mixed `Description`. Put the formula in a Definition, the decimal or null return contract in a Specification, and the Monday reporting practice in a Convention. Link the pages where readers need to move between answers. |
67	| [Service registry](../assets/type-review-example/services.md) | Which team owns each production service today? The table owns the current service-to-team mapping and is updated as membership or ownership changes. | Accept `ServiceRegistry`. Readers can find the inventory by its established project type, and each entry answers the same question.                                                                                                  |
68	
69	## The index
70	
71	A scheduling index can list a Definition of retry limits beside the
72	Specification of what a client sees while waiting. A directory can contain
73	both. A root index can lead through nested indexes to either page.
74	
75	**Guidelines:**
76	
77	- SHOULD list concepts directly at the root while readers can select an answer there. Add a nested index when readers need to choose among a subject's subquestions. OKF permits a directory without an index.
78	- SHOULD link a subject index from its parent, state its scope and give each locally owned decision a descriptive route there. A caller with a specific question can link straight to the owning section.
79	- SHOULD keep rules at their typed owner and use indexes for navigation.
80	- SHOULD use Markdown links for index entries so OKF consumers can traverse them offline. An HTML link that works in a browser does not establish an OKF relationship.
81	- SHOULD add a page only when it owns an answer.
82	
83	## The glossary
84	
85	The legacy flat `specs/<domain>.md` convention pairs specs with glossary domain
86	headings. A typed Specification elsewhere creates no obligation to coin a term.
87	A glossary entry can link to a full Definition and still explain enough for a
88	reader to understand the word in context.
89	
90	For example, **Job output** names what one Job produced, even after its record
91	is gone. Three near-misses narrow or shift that meaning:
92	
93	| Candidate      | Likely interpretation       | Where it misleads                                          |
94	| -------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
95	| Output record  | A record that holds output  | Omits which job produced it.                               |
96	| Failure output | The output of a failed job  | Excludes successful jobs.                                  |

# Documentation Structure

## OKF v0.3 requirements

OKF consumers discover typed concepts, assets and reserved navigation files
within one bundle. Untyped Markdown can coexist with concepts. The format
leaves the vocabulary open, so a consumer can encounter a type it has never
seen. See the [OKF v0.3 specification](https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/blob/527e81aff55992be21507e97004286789126f88c/SPEC.md).

**Guidelines:**

- MUST write a concept as UTF-8 Markdown with a YAML 1.2 core-schema mapping between lines containing exactly `---`. Its only universally required field is a nonempty string `type`. Keys must be unique.
- MUST reserve `index.md` and `log.md` at every depth. Nested indexes and logs have no frontmatter. An existing OKF log uses newest-first YYYY-MM-DD headings. Git-backed living docs use the commit history for changes. Leave the optional log out when bootstrapping.
- MAY declare `okf_version: "0.3"`, a title and a description on the root index. Preserve its existing frontmatter when refreshing the index.
- SHOULD edit only the metadata the change affects, preserving existing extension keys and values.

## Choose the subject

A parsing library can keep the accepted input and its error behavior under
parsing even when three modules implement it. Within a product, a capability
can own its history, sharing and platform-specific presentation. Move a common
interaction or terminology decision into shared design when independent
capabilities use it. A design system covers reusable foundations and components.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD start with the decision a reader brings and where they look for it. Choose the owning subject, then choose the page type by the claim it establishes.
- SHOULD distinguish caller guarantees, shared design, implementation, contributing, operations and authority where the readers and decisions differ. Use the project's names, package boundaries and depth.
- SHOULD record a [placement convention](./conventions-and-operations.md#contributor-routes) when contributors face a meaningful choice between subjects.

## Engineering defaults

These recommended types describe the decision the reader needs to make.

| Type              | Reader's decision                                                    | What belongs together                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Definition        | Does this case count, and what does the value mean?                  | A metric's population, eligibility, units, formula and weighting.                                                                         |
| Specification     | Which observable outcome may a consumer rely on?                     | Inputs, results, timing, failure behavior and guarantees for each mode.                                                                   |
| Convention        | Which practice does the team use where several satisfy the contract? | The selected practice, its reason and the alternative it rules out. Lint enforcement leaves this a convention.                            |
| Architecture      | Who owns this responsibility, and how does work cross the boundary?  | Components, control or data flow and dependencies. Identify implemented boundaries, adopted targets and illustrative examples explicitly. |
| Procedure         | Who runs this task and how do they know it succeeded?                | Entry conditions, prerequisites, ordered actions, checks and recovery.                                                                    |
| Policy (optional) | Who may authorize this action or grant an exception?                 | Shared restrictions, exception authority and reopening conditions, when governed independently of any one procedure.                      |

A table of configuration names, consumers and missing-value behavior can be a
single Specification when the reader needs those facts together.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD give each living page one primary type, a meaningful title and a short discovery description.
- SHOULD adopt the engineering vocabulary for a new bundle and preserve established project types and topic directories where readers or tools depend on them.

### Review the declared type

For each path in the validator's type list, write down the reader's question,
the claim this page owns and why the declared type helps the reader find that
claim. If answering requires several independent claims, identify the passages
and their owners. A project-specific name fits when readers use it for one
recognizable purpose and the page is maintained for that purpose.

Try the [type-review example](../assets/type-review-example/index.md). Both
pages have valid type strings. An editor reading their content should reach
these decisions:

| Page                                                          | Reader's question and the claim the page owns                                                                                                        | Editorial decision                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [Notes](../assets/type-review-example/delivery-notes.md)      | How is the rate calculated? What does the API return for a zero denominator? What does the team do on Monday? Each answer can change independently.  | Flag the mixed `Description`. Put the formula in a Definition, the decimal or null return contract in a Specification, and the Monday reporting practice in a Convention. Link the pages where readers need to move between answers. |
| [Service registry](../assets/type-review-example/services.md) | Which team owns each production service today? The table owns the current service-to-team mapping and is updated as membership or ownership changes. | Accept `ServiceRegistry`. Readers can find the inventory by its established project type, and each entry answers the same question.                                                                                                  |

## The index

A scheduling index can list a Definition of retry limits beside the
Specification of what a client sees while waiting. A directory can contain
both. A root index can lead through nested indexes to either page.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD list concepts directly at the root while readers can select an answer there. Add a nested index when readers need to choose among a subject's subquestions. OKF permits a directory without an index.
- SHOULD link a subject index from its parent, state its scope and give each locally owned decision a descriptive route there. A caller with a specific question can link straight to the owning section.
- SHOULD keep rules at their typed owner and use indexes for navigation.
- SHOULD use Markdown links for index entries so OKF consumers can traverse them offline. An HTML link that works in a browser does not establish an OKF relationship.
- SHOULD add a page only when it owns an answer.

## The glossary

The legacy flat `specs/<domain>.md` convention pairs specs with glossary domain
headings. A typed Specification elsewhere creates no obligation to coin a term.
A glossary entry can link to a full Definition and still explain enough for a
reader to understand the word in context.

For example, **Job output** names what one Job produced, even after its record
is gone. Three near-misses narrow or shift that meaning:

| Candidate      | Likely interpretation       | Where it misleads                                          |
| -------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Output record  | A record that holds output  | Omits which job produced it.                               |
| Failure output | The output of a failed job  | Excludes successful jobs.                                  |
| Completed job  | An execution that has ended | Names the execution itself instead of what it left behind. |

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD capture names from code, user-visible interfaces and team usage. Choose a new name whose ordinary meaning fits the concept. A plausible near-match hides the need to look it up.
- SHOULD use an optional cross-subject glossary for active aliases, UI labels and ambiguous terms. Give the minimum distinction, usually one to three sentences, and link to its owning section. Keep calculations, exceptions, procedures and guarantees at that owner.
- SHOULD explain a specialist term where its subject uses it. Group specialist terms in a subject-local Definition when readers consult them together.
- MUST account for every active alias and unique distinction when shortening a glossary, including meanings embedded in paragraphs. Move the distinction to an owner, retain a short finder or document the evidence for retirement in the change review.
- MUST preserve active spellings and disambiguation. Settle old grouping, presentation and heading compatibility [per route](./cross-references.md#preserve-the-reading-route).

## Diagrams

A state-transition diagram explains an observable contract. A diagram of the
producer and worker explains which component owns a transition.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD keep a diagram beside the claim it explains.
- MUST ship linked images with the bundle when readers need them offline.

# Conventions and Operations

## Placing a project rule

Where a violation appears helps identify the reader who needs the rule. A
client receiving a missing field encounters a contract violation. A reviewer
checking directory layout is applying a Convention, even if a linter enforces
it. An operator diagnosing a queue backlog needs the Architecture to identify
the producer and consumer before consulting a recovery Procedure.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD place an observable guarantee in its Specification and a team's choice among conforming practices in its Convention.
- MUST keep the constraint beside its reasoning and link to its existing owner when already documented. A project with architectural decision records MAY link the original record for provenance.

## Permission and execution

A release operator activates a rollout. A device operator checks the
installation and restores service if verification fails. Both procedures can
depend on the same permission to release. When one operator carries out a
single task, a locally scoped permission check can fit directly in its steps.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD extract a Policy when several entry points depend on a permission rule that changes independently.
- MUST identify the adopted scope, exception authority and reopening conditions, and connect every affected entry point, including manual and emergency paths, to the actual authority.
- SHOULD give operators separate procedures when their tasks have different prerequisites, success signals or recovery actions.
- MUST state the local stop condition beside a consequential step. A successful recovery command establishes what ran. Permission to run it comes from the project's authority.
- MUST NOT invent an approver or independent permission rule to populate a type.

## Contributor routes

A contributor guide can direct a new maintainer to the setup procedure and a
reviewer to the same convention used by the linter. Each route leads to one
maintained rule.

**Guidelines:**

- SHOULD document each subject's scope and its nearest confusing neighbor. Give a tie-breaker a contributor can apply to a new claim and explain when to add a subject. For instance, a worker-pool cap belongs with dispatch internals unless it promises an outcome to callers.
- SHOULD link the placement convention from durable human and agent entry points and update it when responsibility moves. Link editable callers directly to their governing section.

4	description: Which job states callers see, when a failure is retried and what happens at exhaustion.
5	---
6	
7	# Job outcomes and retries
8	
9	## States
10	
11	A job is `queued` when created, `running` from the moment a worker claims it, and ends
12	in `succeeded`, `failed`, or `cancelled`.
13	
14	```mermaid
15	stateDiagram-v2
16	    [*] --> queued
17	    queued --> running: a worker claims it
18	    queued --> cancelled: cancelled before it starts
19	    running --> succeeded: the attempt exits 0
20	    running --> failed: the last attempt exits non-zero
21	    running --> queued: the attempt failed and a retry remains
22	    running --> cancelled: cancelled mid-run
23	```
24	
25	A cancelled job receives no automatic retry, even if retries remain.
26	A job cancelled while running keeps whatever output its attempt had already written.
27	The product does not roll it back.
28	
29	The [lifecycle decision and cancellation test](./cancellation-evidence.txt)
30	cover the case where retries remain. The test cancels a running job with two
31	retries left and observes an empty attempt queue. It does not observe the
32	external process. A client choosing an output-read timeout still needs a
33	shutdown guarantee from that process.
34	
35	## Attempts and retries
36	
37	A failed attempt is retried up to three times, at one, five, and twenty-five minutes
38	after the failure. The job stays `queued` between attempts, so a job waiting on a
39	retry is indistinguishable from a job waiting on a free worker.
40

description: Which job states callers see, when a failure is retried and what happens at exhaustion.

# Job outcomes and retries

## States

A job is `queued` when created, `running` from the moment a worker claims it, and ends
in `succeeded`, `failed`, or `cancelled`.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued
    queued --> running: a worker claims it
    queued --> cancelled: cancelled before it starts
    running --> succeeded: the attempt exits 0
    running --> failed: the last attempt exits non-zero
    running --> queued: the attempt failed and a retry remains
    running --> cancelled: cancelled mid-run
```

A cancelled job receives no automatic retry, even if retries remain.
A job cancelled while running keeps whatever output its attempt had already written.
The product does not roll it back.

The [lifecycle decision and cancellation test](./cancellation-evidence.txt)
cover the case where retries remain. The test cancels a running job with two
retries left and observes an empty attempt queue. It does not observe the
external process. A client choosing an output-read timeout still needs a
shutdown guarantee from that process.

## Attempts and retries

A failed attempt is retried up to three times, at one, five, and twenty-five minutes
after the failure. The job stays `queued` between attempts, so a job waiting on a
retry is indistinguishable from a job waiting on a free worker.

A job that exhausts its retries receives no further automatic attempts. It ends
`failed`, carrying the last attempt's exit status and the tail of its output. See
[which output survives pruning](./jobs.md#output-and-pruning) to retrieve an attempt's output later.

The dashboard shows this limit as **Retries remaining**. For counting the initial
attempt separately, see the [attempt budget](./attempts.md#attempt-budget).

rule can select, so a job that never finishes never notifies —

exactly one channel. A channel serves many rules, so disabling a channel

The release operator uses a checkout of the release revision with production
deployment access. Only the release operator may deploy or roll back, even when

schema and the old code tolerates it, because every migration here is written to be

window where live code queries columns that do not exist yet.

deployed on its own to pick up a fix: the two packages share `shared/`, and a split
deploy runs two versions of it against one queue.

five minutes and confirm queued jobs are being claimed. A release that broke the

already removed data. If it
did, stop and hand the restore to the on-call operator. Deploying an older
revision cannot bring the data back.

For a code rollback, use the recorded previous revision that works with the
current schema:


Leave the migration in place. Destructive changes have separate expand and
contract migrations so the earlier code can run against the expanded schema.
Roll back to the revision before the contract and correct the schema with a
forward migration.

# Job creation and history

## Templates and schedules

A **Job Template** carries a name, the work to run, and an optional schedule. The name is
unique across the account and is what job history is grouped by, so renaming a
template regroups every job it has already produced.

A **Schedule** is the recurrence attached to a template. It produces one job
each time it fires, evaluated in UTC. If the previous job is still running,
the schedule creates a second job. The two can run concurrently within the
worker pool limit. A template with no schedule produces jobs only when someone runs it by hand.

A template is enabled or disabled. A disabled template's schedule does not fire and it
cannot be run by hand, but disabling does not touch jobs already created — a job
queued a moment earlier is still claimed and still runs.

Editing a template does not change jobs already created: each job carries a copy of
the work it was created with, so a template edited while a job is queued runs the old
definition once more.

## Creating a job

A run creates a job, one execution of a template. A firing schedule and a manual
run produce the same record. Only the job's `trigger` field distinguishes them.

A run returns a queued job. A saturated pool can delay its start indefinitely.
A repeated worker claim cannot start a second copy of that job. The
[dispatch boundary](./dispatch.md) explains how all producers share capacity.
See [job outcomes](./outcomes.md#states) for the states a caller can observe.

## Output and pruning

A job's record is pruned thirty days after it ends. Its job output outlives the record
and is addressed by the job's identifier, so a link to output written last quarter
still resolves once the job it came from is gone. Earlier attempts' output is
pruned with the record.

## What scheduling does not do

A job does not trigger another job. There is no dependency graph, no fan-out, and no
"run this once that succeeds" — a template needing a second step runs it inside its
own work.

# Directory Structure

The API and worker are the two deployable **Packages**. Each runs in its own
environment. This convention governs the modules each package contains or imports.

The general discipline — put shared logic at the lowest tier with more than one
caller, name a file for what it holds — belongs to the installed code-maintainability
capability. What follows is this repository's own tiers and paths, which nothing
outside it could infer.

## The Tree

```text
<root>
├── api/                       # the API package: creates jobs, serves the dashboard
│   ├── routes/<route>/
│   │   ├── _components/       # used by this route only
│   │   └── handler.ts
│   └── _/                     # feature-agnostic modules shared across routes
├── worker/                    # the worker package: claims jobs, runs attempts
└── shared/                    # the few modules both packages import
```

## Tiers

A module sits at the lowest tier that has more than one caller, and MUST NOT be
promoted in anticipation of a second — a module promoted early is one every package
pays to read while one of them uses it.

`shared/` MUST stay deliberate. A module there is imported by two deployables that
run in separate processes, so a change to it changes both at once. It belongs there only
when both packages need the same _behaviour_, never merely the same shape.

The import direction is one-way: `api/` and `worker/` MAY import `shared/`; `shared/`
MUST NOT import either, and the two packages MUST NOT import each other. Each
production package contains only its own modules and shared dependencies. A
cross-package import can compile in the checkout and fail in the deployed process.

## Naming

A file is named for what it holds, in kebab-case; a directory, for the thing its files
are about. A route directory MUST match the URL segment it serves — the router derives
one from the other, so a mismatch is a 404 nobody can see in review.

`_`-prefixed directories are not routed. Anything under `routes/` without the prefix
becomes a URL, so a helper dropped there unprefixed is published.

title: Publishing a post
description: What publish writes, when the deploy hook fires, and what the author sees when it doesn't.
---

# Publishing a post

What happens after a post is published spans two files — `server/app.ts`
and `server/deploy-hook.ts` — and one decision worth explaining once rather
than re-deriving at either call site.

## The three steps

Publishing a post is three steps, in order:

1. Write a `revisions` row — a snapshot of the post's title and body at the
   moment of publish. See [what a revision snapshots](./revisions.md#what-a-revision-snapshots).
2. Flip the post's `status` to `published`.
3. Call the site's `deployHookUrl`.

The first two are a single logical write: either both happen or neither
does. The third is best-effort — a site's deploy hook is usually a webhook
on someone else's static host (Vercel, Netlify, and similar all expose
one), and those are occasionally slow or briefly unavailable.

By the time the deploy hook call runs, the post and its revision are
already committed. Rolling that back because a webhook timed out would
throw away real work over a problem that's usually transient and, worse,
outside this app's control entirely.

## What the author sees

The publish response carries `deployTriggered: boolean`, and the editor
shows the author which case they're in:

- hook fired: "Published. The site will rebuild shortly."
- hook didn't fire: "Published, but the deploy didn't fire — you may need
  to trigger it yourself."

Either way the post and its revision are already live in this app; what's
uncertain is only whether the static site rebuilt. See
[recovering a missed build](./guides/desk.md#missed-build) for what to do
about the second case.

This app makes no promise about how long after a deploy hook is accepted
the rebuilt site actually goes live — that depends on the host's own build
queue, which this app never observes. The host's dashboard is the only
place to check that.

## The retry policy

The deploy hook call gets three attempts, with a linear backoff between
them. That's tuned for "a cold serverless function taking a moment to wake
up," not for a target that's genuinely down — three attempts a few hundred
milliseconds apart won't save a publish from a deploy hook that's been
deleted or misconfigured. When every attempt fails, `deploy-hook.ts` logs
the exhaustion at `error` (there's no error tracker on the API side to hand
it to instead — see `shared/logger.ts`) and returns `{ ok: false }` rather
than throwing, so the route above always gets a definite answer either way.

## Correcting a bad publish

There's no unpublish button in this cut of the product. The revision a
publish writes is a record of what went out, not an undo mechanism —
reverting live content means editing the post back to the previous
revision's text and publishing again, which writes a new revision of its
own.

# Revision records

## What a revision snapshots

Publish writes a `revisions` row holding a snapshot of the post's title and
body at the moment of publish — see [publishing a post](./publishing.md).
A draft save updates the post without adding a snapshot; only a publish
creates one.

A post becomes published together with its snapshot, in the same
transaction, so a failed deploy hook never leaves one without the other —
the published post and its revision stay in place regardless of whether the
site's build actually fired.

## How the Revisions screen reads them back

The screen groups snapshots by post. Each group's heading uses the post's
*current* title; each row uses the title that post had *at the moment of
that publish* — editing a post's title afterward relabels the group but
leaves every past snapshot's row showing what that publish actually called
it.

Within a post, revisions are listed newest first. Ordering falls back to
the revision's id when two publishes land in the same second — `created_at`
only resolves to the second, and two publishes within one second are
ordinary, so the higher id, the one written later, sorts first (see the
revisions route in `server/app.ts`). Groups themselves come out ordered by
whichever post was published most recently.

# Recovering a missed build

## Missed build

A failed deploy hook does not undo the publish — the post and its revision
are already committed by the time the hook is called, so the author's
content is live in this app either way. What's missing is the site's
rebuild.

Open the site's hosting dashboard and check its queue for this publication.
If a build for it is queued or running, stop and follow that build.
Otherwise, trigger a rebuild from the host dashboard. Publishing the post
again also calls the deploy hook, but it writes another revision even when
nothing changed, so prefer the host dashboard's rebuild when one is
available.

The [receipt from Acme's release](../receipts/hook-17.txt) is the record
used when support reviews that release.

# Placing a documentation change

## Choose a subject

Put a rule where the person making the decision would look for it:

- Publishing owns what happens when an author publishes — the revision
  write, the status flip, the deploy hook call and what the author sees
  when the hook doesn't fire. For a change to any of those, update
  [publishing a post](../publishing.md).
- Revision records owns what gets snapshotted and how the Revisions screen
  presents it back — ordering, grouping and which title appears where. For
  a change to any of those, update [revision records](../revisions.md).
- Recovering a missed build owns what an author or support does once a
  build didn't happen. Keep its path and `## Missed build` heading working:
  a printed support card links to it directly.

Add a subject when readers bring an independent question with no current
owner. Link it from the root index and distinguish it from its nearest
neighbor here.

# AGENTS.md

## What this project is

A small hosted CMS. An author signs in — session handling lives outside this
cut of the product, so there's no sign-in screen here and the API reads who
the author is from what the session boundary forwards — and manages one or
more customer sites from the same account. Each site has its own posts;
opening a post gives you a full-page editor with a title, a body, a draft
save, and a publish action. Publishing snapshots the post into a revision and
calls the site's deploy hook so the static build actually goes out.

The sidebar carries two sections, Posts and Revisions, and shows which author
is signed in underneath them. There's no dashboard, no settings page, and no
onboarding flow yet.

## How the code is organized

`src/` is the SPA: `routes/` holds the three real screens (a per-site post
list, the post editor, and that site's revision history) plus the shell they
render inside, `components/` holds
what's reusable across more than one of them, `lib/` is where a cross-cutting
concern — the API client, the query client, consent, analytics — gets exactly
one home, and `queries/` holds the TanStack Query option factories, one
export per file, grouped by the resource they read or write rather than by
the screen that happens to call them first.

`server/` is the API: a thin Hono app in `app.ts`, the Drizzle schema and its
generated SQL migrations under `db/`, and the deploy-hook call in its own
module because it's the one thing in this app that talks to somebody else's
infrastructure and needed a retry policy to go with it.

`shared/` is the one thing both sides import — right now just the logger.
Anything that earns a place there has to make sense with zero DOM APIs and
zero Node APIs in scope, since it's bundled into the browser build and run
directly by the API both.

Read `README.md` for the full command list and layout before touching either
side.

## How changes are made

Nothing lands on `main` directly. Sketch the change and get it agreed on
before writing it — a plan is a much cheaper place to catch a misunderstood
requirement than a finished diff is. A pull request gets reviewed by someone
other than whoever wrote it, and it merges once that review has nothing left
to raise and the checks in `README.md` are green.

The [maintenance decisions](maintenance/decisions.md) record agreed work.

Keep a pull request to the problem it set out to solve. Renaming something
you noticed in passing, reformatting a file you didn't otherwise touch, or
folding in an unrelated fix makes the diff harder to review for the same
reason it was harder to write: two changes being reasoned about as though
they were one. Split it, or leave the rest for its own change.

## Publishing, briefly

Publish does three things, in order: write a revision snapshot of the post's
current title and body, flip the post to `published`, and call the site's
deploy hook. The first two are one transaction; the third is best-effort — a
site's deploy hook lives on somebody else's infrastructure, and a slow or
briefly-down webhook shouldn't cost the author their published content. The
API reports whether the deploy actually fired (`deployTriggered`) and the
editor tells the author which case they're in, rather than pretending publish
either fully succeeded or fully failed. `docs/deploy-hooks.md` has the retry
policy and the reasoning behind it; read it before changing
`server/deploy-hook.ts` or the publish route that calls it.

The revision written by step one is what the Revisions screen reads back, so
a change to what publish snapshots changes what that screen shows.
